breakfast.name: Croissant
breakfast.description: Buttery, flaky French pastry with hundreds of delicate layers. Symbol of French baking
instructions: Make dough: Mix flour, salt, sugar, yeast, and water until shaggy
Knead 5 minutes, refrigerate 30 minutes
Pound cold butter into thin sheet
Roll dough into rectangle, place butter in center
Fold dough over butter envelope-style
Refrigerate 30 minutes
Perform 4 letter folds (turn 90°, roll, fold): refrigerate 30 min between each
After final fold, refrigerate overnight
Roll dough 1/8 inch thick, cut into triangles
Roll triangles from base to point to form crescents
Let rise 2 hours at room temperature
Brush with egg wash
Bake at 400°F for 20-25 minutes until golden
breakfast.notes: Lamination (folding butter into dough) creates the layers. Keeping butter cold is essential
breakfast.fun_fact: Despite the name, croissants originated in Austria and were brought to France by Marie Antoinette
alternatives: Store-bought puff pastry to save time
Chocolate croissant (pain au chocolat) with filling

items.name: Cold unsalted butter
items.note: Keep it cold — the key to flaky layers

stepHelp: Just bring it together until there's no dry flour left — you'll develop the gluten more with kneading, not by overmixing here.
The dough should feel smooth and slightly elastic. Chilling relaxes the gluten so it's easier to roll later.
Between two sheets of parchment, pound and roll cold butter into an even rectangle about half the size of your rolled-out dough. If it starts to soften, chill it again before continuing.
Roll the dough about twice the size of your butter block so you have enough to fully enclose it.
Fold the dough's sides over the butter like closing an envelope, pinching the seams to fully seal it in — no butter should be exposed.

Each fold: roll the dough into a long rectangle, then fold it in thirds like a letter. Always refrigerate 30 minutes between folds — this is what builds the hundreds of layers, and skipping the chilling makes the butter melt into the dough instead of staying in sheets.
Roll evenly in one direction, then rotate and roll the other way to keep the thickness consistent. Long, narrow triangles roll into a better crescent shape than short wide ones.
Stretch the triangle gently as you roll toward the point — this creates more visible layers and the classic curved shape when you tuck the ends under.
They're ready when they look noticeably puffier and jiggle slightly when you nudge the tray — don't rush this, it's what makes them light instead of dense.
Deep golden-brown, not pale — that's when the layers have fully set and crisped. A pale croissant will taste doughy in the middle.

variations.title: Pain au Chocolat
variations.text: Roll rectangles instead of triangles, add a stick of chocolate at one end, and roll it up for the classic chocolate version.

variations.title: Almond Croissant
variations.text: Slice a day-old croissant, fill with almond cream, top with sliced almonds, and rebake until golden.

variations.title: Ham & Cheese
variations.text: Add a slice of ham and cheese to the wide end of the triangle before rolling for a savory version.

variations.title: Whole Wheat Lamination
variations.text: Swap up to a third of the flour for whole wheat for a nuttier flavor — the layers will be slightly less airy but still flaky.

variations.title: Mini Croissants
variations.text: Cut smaller triangles for bite-sized croissants — great for a brunch spread, and they bake a few minutes faster.

serveWith.intro: A traditional French breakfast keeps it simple, letting the pastry itself be the centerpiece.

items.title: Good Butter & Jam
items.text: A traditional French breakfast keeps it simple — quality butter and a fruit preserve let the pastry shine.

items.title: Café au Lait
items.text: Strong coffee cut with steamed milk is the classic pairing for the buttery richness.

items.title: Fresh Orange Juice
items.text: The acidity cuts through the butter and wakes up the palate.

items.title: Soft Scrambled Eggs
items.text: For a heartier breakfast, a croissant alongside soft eggs makes a satisfying plate.

items.title: Fruit Salad
items.text: Light and fresh, it balances how rich the croissant is.

expertTips.title: Cold Butter Is Everything
expertTips.text: If the butter softens and starts to melt into the dough at any point, the layers collapse into one greasy mass instead of staying distinct. Chill often, and don't rush.

expertTips.title: Work in a Cool Kitchen
expertTips.text: Lamination is much easier in a cool room — if your kitchen is warm, chill your rolling pin and work surface too.

expertTips.title: Don't Skip the Chill Between Folds
expertTips.text: Each 30-minute rest lets the gluten relax and the butter firm back up — skipping it makes the dough tear and the butter squeeze out.

expertTips.title: Egg Wash Twice
expertTips.text: Brush once before the final rise and again right before baking for the deepest, glossiest golden color.

storage.title: Room Temperature
storage.text: Baked croissants are best the day they're made, but keep in an airtight container at room temperature (not the fridge, which dries them out) for up to 2 days.

storage.title: Freezer
storage.text: Freeze the shaped, unbaked croissants before the final rise — thaw and let rise overnight in the fridge, then bring to room temperature before baking.

storage.title: Reheating
storage.text: Warm day-old croissants in a 300°F oven for 5-8 minutes to re-crisp the layers — a microwave will make them chewy.

breakfast.makeAhead: Croissants are a genuine make-ahead project. Shape the croissants and freeze them right after rolling, before their final rise. The night before you want fresh croissants, move them to the fridge to slowly rise overnight, then let them finish rising at room temperature for about an hour before baking.

faqs.q: Why did my butter leak out while rolling?
faqs.a: The butter likely got too warm. Chill the dough immediately, and next time work faster or in a cooler space, and don't skip the rests between folds.

faqs.q: Can I skip a fold to save time?
faqs.a: You'll get fewer, thicker layers — still tasty, but less of the classic shatter-and-flake texture. Four folds is the sweet spot for the traditional result.

faqs.q: How do I know they've risen enough before baking?
faqs.a: They should look visibly puffed and jiggle slightly when the tray is nudged — under-risen croissants bake dense and heavy.

faqs.q: Is this really an all-day project?
faqs.a: Yes, mostly due to chilling and rising time (most of it hands-off) — active work is closer to an hour total spread across the day, or split it over two days.

lunch.name: Coq au Vin (Chicken in Wine)
lunch.description: Classic Burgundian dish with chicken braised in red wine with mushrooms, pearl onions, and lardons
ingredients: 1 whole chicken (4 lbs), cut into pieces
instructions: Cook pancetta in large pot until crispy, set aside
Brown chicken pieces in pancetta fat, set aside
Sauté pearl onions and mushrooms, set aside
Add garlic and tomato paste to pot, cook 2 minutes
Deglaze with red wine, scraping up browned bits
Add broth, bay leaves, thyme
Return chicken to pot with carrots
Bring to simmer, cover, braise 45 minutes
Add pearl onions and mushrooms
Braise uncovered 30 more minutes
Chicken should be tender and falling off bones
Season with salt and pepper
Garnish with parsley and pancetta
Serve with crusty bread or egg noodles
lunch.notes: The long braise develops deep flavors. Don't rush this dish
lunch.fun_fact: Coq au Vin was born out of necessity - using old roosters tough enough to require long cooking

dinner.name: Bouillabaisse (Provençal Fish Stew)
dinner.description: Luxurious Provençal seafood stew from Marseille with saffron, fennel, and orange. Served with rouille and crusty bread
ingredients: 2 lbs mixed white fish (sea bass, halibut, monkfish)
instructions: Heat oil in large pot over medium heat
Sauté fennel and onion until soft
Add garlic and cook 1 minute
Add tomatoes and wine, simmer 5 minutes
Add broth, bay leaf, thyme, orange zest
Simmer 20 minutes to develop flavors
Steep saffron in 1/4 cup warm broth, add to pot
Increase heat to medium-high
Add firm fish pieces first
Simmer 5 minutes
Add mussels and shrimp
Cook 5-8 minutes until shellfish opens and fish is cooked
Season with salt and pepper
Serve in wide bowls with broth, crusty bread, and generous rouille
dinner.notes: Use highest quality fish and shellfish. Authentic bouillabaisse uses specific Mediterranean fish
dinner.fun_fact: Bouillabaisse is protected by an official recipe and charter in Marseille, France

snacks.name: Macarons (Almond Meringue Cookies)
snacks.description: Delicate French almond cookies with smooth dome shape, filled with ganache or buttercream
instructions: Sift powdered sugar and almond flour together 3 times
Beat egg whites until soft peaks form
Gradually add granulated sugar while beating
Continue beating until stiff, glossy peaks form
Add vanilla and food coloring
Gently fold dry ingredients into meringue in 3 additions
Pipe 1-inch discs onto parchment paper using piping bag
Let sit at room temperature 30 minutes (shells form)
Bake at 300°F for 15-18 minutes (bottoms should be set)
Cool completely on baking sheet
Pipe filling (ganache or buttercream) on flat side of half
Sandwich with another macaron
Let set 24 hours for best texture
snacks.notes: Macarons are temperamental - humidity affects success. Precise measurements critical
snacks.fun_fact: Macarons originated in Italy but became famous in France, especially Paris where Ladurée and Pierre Hermé are legendary
alternatives: Store-bought almond flour to save time
Pre-made filling instead of homemade ganache

desserts.name: Crème Brûlée (Burnt Cream)
desserts.description: Silky vanilla custard with caramelized sugar topping. Iconic French dessert
instructions: Heat cream with vanilla bean (scrape seeds into cream) until steaming
Let steep 30 minutes
Whisk egg yolks with 1/4 cup sugar until pale
Slowly temper yolks by adding warm cream while whisking
Strain through fine mesh
Add salt
Pour into ramekins
Place ramekins in water bath (hot water halfway up sides)
Bake at 325°F for 30-40 minutes (centers should jiggle slightly)
Cool completely, then refrigerate at least 4 hours
Just before serving, sprinkle remaining sugar on top of each
Use torch to caramelize sugar until deep amber
Let cool 1 minute before serving (sugar hardens to crack)
desserts.notes: Water bath is essential for creamy texture. Don't overbake
desserts.fun_fact: Crème Brûlée became trendy globally in the 1980s-90s due to its elegant presentation and simple preparation
alternatives: Skip torch and use oven broiler
Add liqueur to custard for different flavor

drinks.name: Café au Lait (Coffee with Milk)
drinks.description: Strong coffee mixed with hot milk in equal proportions. Traditional French breakfast drink
instructions: Brew strong coffee (darker roast preferred)
Heat milk until steaming
Pour coffee into large bowl or cup
Pour hot milk into coffee simultaneously
Mix well
Add sugar if desired
Drink from bowl using bread to dip (traditional)
drinks.notes: The ratio of coffee to milk is crucial - true café au lait is 50/50
drinks.fun_fact: French breakfast culture revolves around café au lait and croissants

drinks.name: Bordeaux Wine
drinks.description: Premium red wine from Bordeaux region, typically blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
instructions: Serve at room temperature (16-18°C)
Open 30 minutes before serving to let breathe
Pour into wine glass
Appreciate color and aroma
Sip slowly, noting tannins and fruit notes
drinks.notes: Quality Bordeaux improves with age and can be cellared for decades
drinks.fun_fact: Bordeaux wines are among the world's most prestigious and expensive wines
